# **A: Summary of application (B ‐ H)**

In the time it takes you to read this summary, your body will have synthesised over 5 quintillion proteins. Proteins are the fundamental building blocks of life that orchestrate the complex symphony of biological processes. The chains of amino acid residues are shaped by water, intricately folding to minimise the disruption of hydrophobic residues and maximise hydrophilic interaction within this (sticky) network. It is truly remarkable that despite all the attention paid to proteins, one aspect of these marvels of molecular engineering is constantly overlooked: their surprising fragility. Combining estimates of hydrolysis (i.e. disintegration by water) from laboratory heating experiments with evidence from battered and bruised ancient proteins from archaeological sites leads to the shocking conclusion that within 7 hours, 1 in every 500 of your newly minted proteins will have snapped in two; “your water is a sore decayer…” *Hamlet Act 5, Scene 1\.*

What, which, how, when, where? 

The truth is \- we simply don't know. Our understanding of the chemical stability of peptide bonds has advanced remarkably little in the 70 years since Walter Schroeder highlighted the problem to Linus Pauling [(Schroeder, 1951\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/YGtPk). Predictions of protein stability have a long history but the problem has resisted all attempts to derive a generalised model for peptide-bond hydrolysis. 

ChronoProtein seeks to tackle this question head-on. It will:-

1) develop new algorithms and approaches to help data-mine ancient proteomes and interpret degraded peptides, proteins and proteomes;   
2) use this enhanced data to inform molecular simulations using quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics approaches.  
3) Develop robust kinetic models, by integrating paleoclimate data into protein degradation models applied across datasets spanning from seconds to millions of years and temperatures from 0 \- 150 oC.

1-3 will ultimately deliver:-

(a) for the first time, a Hydrolysis Index of 402 peptide bonds,   
(b) improved methods for dating and authenticating ancient samples, and   
(c) new insights into protein longevity and degradation.

ChronoProtein will enable palaeoproteomics to take its proper place in leading new developments in the analysis of degraded proteomes. In doing so it will help shed light into many different shadowy corners \- from prebiotic chemistry to synthetic protein design, food science to forensics, ancient proteins in fossils, to the old proteins within us.

# **B: Scientific achievements/discoveries**

I was brought to Denmark with a DNRF Niels Bohr Chair as the so-called ‘father of biomolecular archaeology’ (*sic*). Over the last 5 years, I have tried to **bridge multiple disciplines** including archaeology, palaeontology, biochemistry, data science, palaeography and codicology, helping to establish the School of Archaeology at UCPH and having helped get Heritage Science on the Danish roadmap, acting as Danish coordinator of IPERION and [E-RIHS](https://sites.google.com/e-rihs.dk/e-rihs-dk).

My team has developed new computational methods for analysing ancient proteins, building on my earlier work on protein degradation modelling (Paper 1 of Included papers) and racemization (Paper 2), with two further papers in review building on work assessing protein degradation through site-specific deamidation patterns of PhD student Abigail Ramsøe (2021) *Scientific Reports,* 11: 7795\.

I have been instrumental in establishing the field of **biocodicology**, which integrates biological analysis into codicological studies (Paper 3 of Included papers). A paper in *Heritage Science* (Fiddyment et al., 2019, 7: 35*)* provides a field guide for the biological analysis of parchment, opening new avenues for understanding the production and use of historical documents. This discipline has grown even faster than another core technology I helped develop, ZooMS (Fig. 1), our paper on standardising nomenclature (2021, *Journal of Proteomics*, 235: 104041\) reflects ongoing leadership in this area.

Ten years ago we pioneered the study of dietary proteins from dental calculus (Warinner et al., 2014, *Nature genetics,* 46: 336), and subsequently coprolites and in the groundbreaking work by my PhD students Jessie Hendy (pottery) and Theis Trolle-Jensen (chewing gum). Growing integration of these two approaches over the next decade explains the rationale behind our database-independent ***Orthrus*** pipeline developed by PhD student Chiang, which is designed to unite metagenomic and metaproteomic data. 

Despite a few hand-picked examples of palaeoproteomics as a tool for evolutionary studies, e.g. placing *Gigantopithecus* as an early diverging pongine *(*Welker F et al. 2019 *Nature*, 576: 262*)*, even the reconstruction of a protein from an extinct lineage of giant thunderbirds (Paper 4 of Included papers) highlighted by [DeepMind](https://deepmind.google/discover/blog/solving-the-mystery-of-how-an-ancient-bird-went-extinct/), is limited in more closely related taxa (e.g. Grealy A. *et al.* 2023 *Nat. Comm*. 14, 914). Nevertheless, our predictions of the role of mineral surfaces (Paper 3 of Included papers) were proved correct in the first recorded intact Miocene peptide (*eLife*, 2023\) last year. 

**Figure 1 Bibliographic analysis**: Amino acid geochronology stretches back to the 1960’s. The past 5 years have seen rapid growth in ancient protein analysis (palaeoproteomics), peptide mass fingerprinting (ZooMS), and biological studies of parchment (biocodicology), which are all areas that I helped develop with my students and postdocs.

# C: Project description

As a young postdoctoral student in the early 1990s, studying the survival of ancient proteins and their application to amino acid racemization geochronology (AAR), the rate of chemical hydrolysis of proteins was essential information. I remember my shock at realising that the relative stability of different peptide bonds was unknown. I puzzled the problem a little myself [(Collins *et al.*, 1995, 1999\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/6OfUu+yitn), but it was too challenging, so I put it aside, instead helping found a new field which in 2014 [(Cappellini, Collins and Gilbert, 2014\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/WJZ6) we named **‘palaeoproteomics’**. Palaeoproteomics uses soft-ionisation mass-spectrometry to analyse and identify proteins extracted from ancient materials. While analytical technologies continue to rapidly advance, ancient proteins persist as degraded and modified (poly)peptide fragments which conventional proteomic analysis is not designed for [(Palomo *et al.*, 2023; Yun Chiang, Welker and Collins, 2024\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/i6jqC+TI0xe).

ChronoProtein seeks to address this decades-old problem and generate realistic models of survival by combining palaeoproteomics, Amino Acid Racemization (AAR) geochronology and multiscale molecular simulations. Protein mass spectrometry conducted on degradation time series and ancient archaeological proteomes will inform us about site-specific hydrolysis and provide high-quality MS2 spectra to train transformer-based *de novo* models [(Eloff *et al.*, 2023\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/nV27a). These will help develop and refine two new analytical approaches, *Orthrus* and *Vidx*, that will significantly enhance the analysis of degraded proteomes. AAR will provide multiple estimates of the rates of hydrolysis, racemization and decomposition of individual amino acids in fossil samples. Multiscale molecular simulations will inform us on reasons behind relative rates of hydrolysis at specific sites, and the role of local effects.

ChronoProtein will combine these to derive the first-ever, complete Hydrolysis Index (*IH*). All this information will then be built into a 2nd order polymer degradation model (*ModulAAR*) which will enable estimates of the fractional amounts of buried (intra-crystalline, closed system) and exposed (inter-crystalline, open system) proteins in ancient samples, estimate the amounts of chemically available water for hydrolysis, and relative rates and therefore (activation energies of) hydrolysis, racemization and diagenesis rates of amino acids. As a result, ChronoProtein allows a unified understanding of protein degradation across geological to picosecond timescales, from the depths of mammalian evolution to the dynamics of modern biomedical interventions.

**Palaeoproteomics and the problem with conventional analysis of degraded proteins:** It took oncologists (7) to point out that the explosive growth of **palaeoproteomics** now represents our largest dataset of damaged and modified proteins. Unfortunately, this damage means that conventional software struggles to identify peptides, even from a pure solution of heat-degraded β-lactoglobulin (β-LG [(Palomo *et al.*, 2023\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/i6jqC)). Less than **5%** of typical palaeoproteomic MS2 spectra are identified [(c.f. 25% in modern proteomes Yun Chiang, Welker and Collins, 2024; Fig 2\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/TI0xe/?prefix=c.f.%2025%25%20in%20modern%20proteomes&suffix=%3B%20Fig%202). This is why new *de novo* sequencing approaches are so powerful [(Zhou *et al.*, 2024\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/BVn7). They attempt to assign amino acid sequences to every MS2 spectrum. If the target is both (i) simple and (ii) known \- as is the case for much **experimental diagenesis** [(B. Demarchi *et al.*, 2013; Crisp *et al.*, 2013; Sakalauskaite *et al.*, 2021\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/8jpC+YeLa+gVCq), ancient collagen, fossil enamel, shell and eggshell proteomes \- the quality of all these *de novo* predictions can be explored. In the case of heat-degraded β-LG, *Casanovo 1.0* [(Yilmaz *et al.*, 2022\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/9EYe3) correctly assigned 25% of MS2 spectra. An equal fraction were *hopeless* hallucinations, but the remaining 50% contained unique motifs of the target protein (β-LG). These 50% therefore offer both a glimpse into the workings of the *de novo* model and additional sequence data. Largely ignored by conventional software, these are now the targets of my new approach to MS2 spectra analysis called *Valley Indexing* (*Vidx*, patent being drafted).

***Valley Indexing*** **(*Vidx*)** is an orthogonal analysis tool which can use outputs from various *de novo* and *open search* tools to score peptides. I developed *Vidx* to analyse heated β-LG experiments [(Palomo *et al.*, 2023\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/i6jqC), which are so simple that *hallucinations* (predicted sequences not found in the original experiment) were easy to spot. *Vidx* will be applied to *Orthrus* output from palaeoproteomics studies to help identify high-quality non-tryptic spectra with post-translational modifications (PTMs) in order to develop a palaeoproteomics-focused training set.  
***Orthrus***: Chiang (PostDoc2) will develop her *Orthrus* pipeline to map cleavage sites and modifications. *Orthrus* is named after the two-headed mythological dog because it incorporates both *de novo* and *open-search* strategies. The spectra identified by the *de novo* are assembled into contigs used in the open search step. *Orthrus* significantly increases the identification rate of MS2 protein spectra from ancient samples (Fig. 2). Over the course of ChronoProtein, PostDoc2 and PostDoc3 will explore alternative *de novo* and open search solutions [(e.g. Kong *et al.*, 2017; Altenburg, Muth and Renard, 2021; Lazear, 2023\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/OxoI+90SMw+Mxc9/?prefix=e.g.,,). Transformer models are making significant and incremental gains in the sequencing of MS2 fragments using Data Dependent Acquisition (DDA) [(Yilmaz *et al.*, 2022; Ebrahimi and Guo, 2023; Eloff *et al.*, 2023; Yang *et al.*, 2023; J. Xia *et al.*, 2024; Lee and Kim, 2024; Petrovskiy *et al.*, 2024; Zhou *et al.*, 2024\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/9EYe3+OVJv+NxzG+BVn7+nV27a+Sagh+8d9w+gEQj), with the first attempts of Data Independent Acquisition (DIA) being promising [(Ebrahimi and Guo, 2023; Sanders *et al.*, 2024\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/OVJv+u9CD). DIA is ultimately preferable as an analytical approach as it is comprehensive and should reveal more rare modified sites which will never be queried in the more selective DDA analysis.

**Ancient Proteomes:** *Bird eggshell* (e.g. Fig. 3\) is widely studied as a model system for biomineralization, more than 800 proteins have been identified, but two calcium-binding proteins usually dominate [(Le Roy *et al.*, 2021\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/wCvEl). *Mollusc shells* have been used for amino acid geochronology [(Demarchi, 2020\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/wfxD5) for decades, but their proteomes are only now being characterised [(Sakalauskaite *et al.*, 2020\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/28gmf). *Dental enamel* has a very small proteome but, as the most highly mineralised tissue in the animal kingdom, it is robust and widely used for sexing [(Parker *et al.*, 2018\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/ZajJF) and phylogeny [(Welker *et al.*, 2019\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/lXpBy). *Bone* and *dentine* are open systems, composed of complex proteomes that are dominated by collagen and that are generally studied for phylogenetic research [(H. Xia *et al.*, 2024\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/2rIP). Mineralized collagen is widely studied in archaeological samples, forms the basis of ZooMS [(Buckley *et al.*, 2009\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/XrNG) and is a long-lived protein which becomes embrittled in bone with age.

ChronoProtein will collaborate with some of the leading experts in mass spectrometry and amino acid analysis, including Jensen, (SDU), Tokarski (Bordeaux), Zubarev (Karolinska), Cramer (Reading), and Penkman (York), giving us access to a variety of ionisation methods (MALDI, electrospray, direct infusion), combined with different MS platforms (Quad TOF, Orbitrap, FT-ICR/MS, LAP-MALDI) and fragmentation modes (CID, HCD), this potential will be leveraged for analysing complex mixtures, performing mass defect analysis, and accessing elemental composition and fine structure information.

**Amino Acid Racemization (AAR) geochronology**: Overlooked by the palaeoproteomics community, a 60-year-long archive of geochronological amino acid analysis (hereafter **AAR**) from the geosciences [(Wehmiller and Pellerito, 2015; *Amino acid racemization data*, 2024\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/x7UMh+5F5D), provides data on the extent of epimerization and hydrolysis of amino acids in fossils. AAR, once derided as ‘some kind of a joke’ [(Marshall, 1990\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/nFCt) is slowly but steadily gaining ground as the clock-like behaviour of protein decay is observed when careful measurements are combined with well-selected samples (Fig. )3. It is a perfect foil for palaeoproteomics as AAR identifies all the amino acids present, helping us to understand problems with extraction and low identification rates linked to degradation. Peptide bond hydrolysis rates change with temperature (Fig. 3c) and the *PastClim* team [(Leonardi *et al.*, 2023\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/cn9rs) gives us the ability to predict thermal histories across the world up to 30Ma ago. Combining AAR, thermal age [(Smith *et al.*, 2003\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/TdCJy) and palaeoproteomics allows ChronoProtein to assemble amino acid hydrolysis, epimerization and decay across a vast range of times and temperatures. This generates bulk and peptide-bond specific rates of hydrolysis and helps to select peptides and proteins for more detailed focus, further experimental degradation studies and multi-scale analysis.

**Hydrolysis Index (*IH*):** At the heart of the ChronoProtein innovations is the estimation of relative rates of hydrolysis of all common amino acid combinations (20 biological amino acids Xxx20-Yyy20, \+ Hydroxyproline), a concept drawn from lessons learnt from the deamidation index (*ID*) [(Robinson and Robinson, 2001\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/zZf1). *ID* was intended as a metric used to estimate the initial single-residue deamidation half-time for proteins, considering all Xxx-Asn-Yyy and XXx-Gln-Yyyn residues. Like ID, *IH* represents an aggregated measure of the hydrolysis potential across all peptide bonds in a protein. However, the most valuable element of the *ID* has been the estimate of the relative rates of deamidation. In a similar manner, the primary goal of *IH* is to derive an estimate of the relative rate of hydrolysis of all possible amino acid combinations. 

**MultiScale molecular simulation:** The role played by higher-order structure in refining rates of deamidation has taken 20 years to develop [(Lawson *et al.*, 2022; Niu *et al.*, 2024\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/28Fh6+ZE6Ie) and this has leant heavily on *ID*. The structure of the protein governs hydrolysis, and our ability to predict **structure** from sequence has massively increased in recent years [(Tunyasuvunakool *et al.*, 2021\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/4r8Zu). We will take a combined approach to explore the role of local effects. **Reactive Force Field (*ReaxFF*)** [(Rahnamoun *et al.*, 2020\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/xhMBz) identifies areas where peptide bonds are under stress, while the **Perturbed Matrix Method (PMM)** delivers detailed electronic insights into these critical regions (e.g. ***PyMM** [(Chen et al., 2023\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/7kn9s)*). The approach balances computational efficiency with accuracy, allowing ChronoProtein to model both large-scale dynamics and localised quantum effects. 

***ModulAAR*** ([https://github.com/Palaeoprot/ModulAAR](https://github.com/Palaeoprot/ModulAAR)) is a developing 2nd-order polymer model with a primary focus on closed system (i.e. intracrystalline proteins) *but* allows for open system (pseudo-first order irreversible) kinetics and can mix both, based upon fractional estimates of open and closed systems[^1]. **Module1 (data extraction)** extracts four components (bound L-amino acids, bound D, free L, and free D for each amino acid) derived from bulk AAR data [(*Amino acid racemization data*, 2024\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/5F5D), enabling model predictions of hydrolysis, racemization and decomposition to be tested over time. Time series are taken directly from laboratory data (WP1a, see below for WP descriptions) and ancient samples with stable temperatures (WP1b) or generated by using thermal histories (WP1c) to normalise samples subject to long-term climate variation to equivalent ‘thermal ages’ [(Smith *et al.*, 2003\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/TdCJy). Data from time series are processed to remove outliers. In **Module2** initial bulk system estimates \- rates of hydrolysis( **k*hyd*** ) and decomposition (**k*decom*** *)*, **Arrhenius parameters *Ea* and *A*** \- are obtained using a scaling approach [(Crisp *et al.*, 2013\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/YeLa) which compares rate differences by scaling the time axes at different temperatures to maximise the overlay of both the decline in total hydrolyzable amino acids (**THAA**) and the increase in free amino acids (**FAA**). In order to estimate the **number of water molecules \[H20\]** in a closed system, the code fits the increase in release of FAA as second-order polymer degradation, taking account of water generated by dehydration reactions*.* **Module3** then uses these bulk systems as the starting point for fitting individual rates of hydrolysis and epimerization for each amino acid in turn, modelling these processes, therefore deriving individual *Ea* and *A* for each measured amino acid. **Module4** will add the estimated activation energies (*Ea*) (data spans 0 \- 150 oC) from Module 3 to *IH*, enabling the use of climate data, currently PastClim [(Leonardi *et al.*, 2023\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/cn9rs), altitude refinement and ground temperature seasonal dampening, to test the rates using all the AAR data which lacked sufficient information to be used to generate the model. As the module generates increased sophistication, each peptide bond of a protein sequence will be scaled using *IH*. **Module5** is a plotting module. **Module6** is planned as an interactive dashboard making the code (already on Google Colab) even more accessible. ***ModulAAR*** is therefore both a tool to generate and test bulk Arrhenius parameters, but over time by adding position specific rates (from *IH*) it can predict the appearance of specific peptides and their extent of racemization which can be explore with more sophisticated computational approaches. 

## **Research Plan**

**WP1: Data mining and analysis of ancient proteomes** (PostDoc1, PostDoc2-Yun Chiang, PhD1, with SDU, PhD with Turin; collaboration, Penkman, Demarchi, Rao, Sakalauskaite, Marin, Ambrose, Welker, Miller, Kaufmann). WP1 includes (i.) assembling AAR data from mineral entrapped (and therefore closed) systems to generate many high-density time series spanning thousands of years across a range of temperatures (PostDoc1), (ii.) Generating ancient proteomic data for closed systems (dental enamel, bird eggshell, mollusc shell) across millions of years, and (iii.) Generating ancient proteomic data for open systems (bone and dentine) across the last 1 million years. Ancient protein datasets overcome the limitations of artificial ageing (WP2) where high temperatures and extreme pHs are used to accelerate rates of peptide-bond hydrolysis but do not accurately predict patterns of protein decay at biological temperatures. PostDoc1 will also compile relevant data from ProteomeXchange. All new AAR data generated by WP1 will be added to the NCEI./NOAA database [(*Amino acid racemization data*, 2024\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/5F5D).

**WP2: Data generation degradation of modern peptides and proteins** PhD1 with SDU, Technician 1-UCPH & Technician 2-SDU, 5% post with York; collaboration Penkman, Demarchi, Sakalauskaite, Tokarski, Zubarev, Cramer, Wang, Priault). WP2 will utilise a diverse range of materials, including eggshell, dental enamel, denatured type I collagen (gelatin) as well as synthetic peptides selected to explore atypically fast or slow rates of decay, solubility, and predicted secondary structural motifs. The refined workflow, based on previous β-LG work enables the identification of multiple hydrolysis events across a range of temperatures: 50, 60, 70, 90, 110, and 140°C for dipeptides and shell powders, and 50, 60, 70, 80, and 90°C for shell proteins, lysates, and synthetic peptides, with low-temperature experiments 50 \- 70°C running for up to \> six years (i.e. beyond the lifetime of the ChronoProtein grant). PhD1 with SDU and PhD2 with Turin will both generate additional data on bone/dental enamel and ancient shell respectively, and these two groups will be providing additional data from ongoing projects with these tissues.

**WP3 Estimating the Hydrolysis Index** (PhD3 Rome, PostDoc2-Yun Chiang, PostDoc3) will develop the *Orthrus* pipeline (PostDoc2) in collaboration with DTU (InstaNovo, PostDoc3) and Bordeaux (ProMeta), to enhance proteomics data analysis generated in WP1 and WP2, maximising the recovery of peptide-bond hydrolysis evidence while minimising false discovery. The workflow will involve ordering samples by thermal age (t10 °C), estimating Khyd for each peptide-bond, refining thermal ages through recursive fitting, developing tissue-specific models for the appearance (Khyd) and decay (Kloss) of every hydrolyzed peptide-bond detected in tissues normalising to a constant t10 °C. The analysis will account for side chain modifications, separately count N- and C-terminal cleavage sites, calculate intrinsic MS peptide detectability, and document trypsin autolysis where applicable. The appearance and loss of cleavage sites will be used to compute the abundance of 401 \~XY\~ peptide-bond pairs and normalise the frequency of bond pairs relative to all identified peptides and the parent proteome. This comprehensive approach will result in the first crude *IH* based on normalised \~XY\~ cleavage site frequency, which will benchmark individual peptide bonds to select peptides for synthesis, experimental decay (WP2) and modelling.

**WP4 Molecular Simulation** (PhD3 Rome with Marco D’Abramo and PostDoc4, PSU). Empirical data gathered in WP1 to WP3 will be complemented by computational techniques to explore peptide-bond hydrolysis. Even though it is difficult to tackle such a problem from a classical point of view there has been some effort in understanding the non-enzymatic peptide-bond breakage in neutral water due to its importance for biological processes [(Kahne and Still, 1988; Radzicka and Wolfenden, 1996; Gorb *et al.*, 2005\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/lWliv+UDxCX+Ofdyy). Our initial focus will be on peptides (e.g. amelogenin cleavage products from amelogenesis; dental enamel) followed by small globular proteins (c-type lectins; eggshell) and finally larger proteins (neuronal pentraxin; eggshell) containing both ordered and disordered regions. PhD3 (w. Rome) will apply quantum mechanics / molecular mechanics (Perturbed Matrix Method) to provide atomistic-level understanding. PostDoc4 will develop and employ empirical reactive force-fields [(ReaxFF, van Duin *et al.*, 2001\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/Zx8t3/?prefix=ReaxFF%2C). The recent integration of ReaxFF with the AMBER protein non-reactive force field [(Rahnamoun *et al.*, 2020\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/xhMBz) provides a hybrid reactive/non-reactive simulation option that greatly increases the accessible time scales for protein/peptide hydrolysis. WP4 data will help to explore positional effects and how they alter *IH*.

**WP5 *ModulAAR*** (PI with all collaborators) is the testbed which integrates all the data from the project and is used to help shape the selection of tissues and proteins for study and peptides for synthesis and modelling.  *ModulAAR* modules which can be used individually or together to explore both AAR and proteomics degradation data. It extends the idea I first developed in Crisp et al. [(2013)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/YeLa/?noauthor=1) of using temporal scaling to approximate kinetic estimates, but is refined by using an explicit 2nd order model of hydrolysis to which known reaction pathways can be added and explored \- currently  DKP and lactam formation, positional specific epimerization, dehydration and deamidation \- in order to predict more detailed model outputs across a wide range of temperatures. 

## **New Insights**

*IH*  will be a fundamental reference point in protein chemistry. Combined with *Ea*, ChronoProtein will provide foundational resources for understanding protein degradation across diverse contexts and timescales. *ModulAAR* enables exploration of the behaviour of protein hydrolysis in a range of open and closed systems, \[H2O\] and (with *IH*) primary sequence in rates of hydrolysis, racemization and decomposition. ReaxFF and PMM will refine these to explore local effects.  Improved degradation kinetics will enhance protein-based **dating methods** and shed light on the behavior of **long-lived proteins.** ChronoProtein will provide new tools for **authentication**, an under-appreciated virtue, but evidenced by the 2022 Nobel Prize for Medicine (for ancient DNA).

## **Impact and redefinition of the field(s) of research**

The development of *IH* will provide a reference point for understanding protein stability and degradation, extending far beyond the narrow field of palaeoproteomics. Deamidation and isomerization of Asn, Asp [(Ugur *et al.*, 2015\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/UEA9H) and isomerization of Ser [(Hoitink *et al.*, 1998; Takahashi, Kobayashi and Oda, 2010; Beatrice Demarchi *et al.*, 2013\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/JqA0u+8i7fC+rTOei) are observed *in vivo* and have physiological consequences [(Boudier-Lemosquet *et al.*, 2021; Lawson, Dekle and Adamczyk, 2022\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/GLQgm+ZvAsh). 

ChronoProtein's tools *ModulAAR*, *Orthrus*, and *Vidx* will enhance the way we analyse AAR and palaeoproteomic datasets and accelerate the discovery of degradation hot- and cold-spots. At their preliminary state of development, the identification rate of MS2 spectra from ancient samples rises from 5% to 50% using *Orthrus* and further up to 75% with *Vidx* \- this should have a transformative impact on studies of ‘old’ proteins. By potentially unlocking the 94% of currently unidentified spectra, we will vastly expand the pool of data available for analysis. Enhanced peptide sequence recovery and associated authentication will significantly increase the number of peptides (and proteoforms) identified from hominin proteomes, allow for the consistent identification of amino acid sites containing sequence heterozygosities [(Madupe *et al.*, 2023\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/PtuK), as well as the recovery of novel single amino acid variants. Together, they will aid in unlocking the full potential of skeletal phylo-proteomic analysis of hominin fossils (Welker Group, UCPH). These tools will also help in explaining the unpredicted persistence of proteins in some subtropical locations [(Peters *et al.*, 2023\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/tsp7s), which will inform the selection of archaeological and palaeontological sites suited for in-depth palaeoproteomic and AAR analysis in the future. Finally, the persistence of peptides into the Mesozoic (65 Ma), although improbable, would profoundly change **palaeontology** in the same way that palaeoproteomics is now transforming **archaeology**.

The development of the multi-scale computational model for predicting protein degradation across different timescales will bridge the gap between laboratory experiments and ancient samples. Using QM/MM on targeted positions will help inform the ReaxFF environment, not least due to the complementarity of PMM and ReaxFF. Unstable regions of intact proteins, and stable peptides formed by decomposition can be explored using synthetic peptides, while predicted patterns of decay can be compared between geological and experimental datasets. This will enable us to test the limits of *IH* due to the role played by local residues and structural effects and also explore specific reaction pathways (e.g. terminal DKP formation) and general effects (e.g. the availability of water in confined systems). 

The creation of a unified analytical approach for comparing degradation processes in ancient and modern samples will foster greater integration between archaeological and biomedical research. This cross-disciplinary impact could lead to new insights in both fields, potentially revealing common principles of protein degradation across vastly different timescales. The results will have practical applications in **forensic science**, particularly in age and post-mortem interval estimations. Insights from ChronoProtein could guide the engineering of **synthetic peptides** and **proteins**. Ancient proteomics often targets long-lived extracellular matrix proteins (EMPs) which have slow turnover [(Hedges *et al.*, 2007; Zhang *et al.*, 2020\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/f2cUg+FIitl) and therefore measurable decay [(Gsell, Veres and Kreplak, 2023\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/UJJqc) which when applied to fresh tissue samples this may challenge current paradigms such as rates of **protein turnover** [(Couppé *et al.*, 2021\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/kTvmk). ChronoProtein's insights will contribute to areas such as atherosclerosis [(Shapiro *et al.*, 1991\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/Gssn), neurodegeneration [(Yeung *et al.*, 2014\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/pUUEE) and arthritis research [(Zhang *et al.*, 2020\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/f2cUg). We have early evidence (Welker and co, unpublished) of differential protein modification and degradation across the human skeleton in a manner synchronous with the relative age of formation of the skeletal elements. The application of *Orthrus* and *Vidx* would then open up the possibility of skeletal age estimation based on proteome degradation. It would be ironic that a response to the products of *chemical decay* [(Dierckx *et al.*, 2024; Hwang *et al.*, 2024\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/jzG1d+RJ48o), was the basis of a current obsession with collagen supplements. 

## **Competitive Edge**

ChronoProtein is a comprehensive, interdisciplinary approach to the long-standing challenge of predicting peptide bond stability across vast timescales. My extensive experience spanning archaeology, chemistry, mass spectrometry, and modelling enables me to successfully coordinate a diverse group of collaborators. Key competitive advantages include:

1. Innovative tools: Development of *InstaNovo*, *ProMeta*, *Orthrus* and *Vidx* to increase ancient peptide spectra identification by an order of magnitude.  
2. Universal Hydrolysis Index (*IH*): Quantifying relative stability of all possible peptide bond combinations, providing a fundamental reference for protein stability across fields.  
3. Multi-scale computational models: enables long-timescale simulations of entire peptide systems ReaxFF with quantum mechanical accuracy for targeted regions, which in turn refines ReaxFF.  
4. Bridging disciplines by analysing ancient proteins alongside modern counterparts.  
5. Unified analytical framework: Standardised protocols and software for comparing degradation processes across timescales.  
6. Extensive collaborative network: Leveraging relationships with experts across relevant fields.

This comprehensive strategy positions ChronoProtein at the forefront of protein degradation research, with potential impacts spanning archaeology, palaeontology, biotechnology, and medicine. By democratising access to advanced protein analysis techniques, we aim to foster innovation across multiple scientific disciplines and finally develop a universal model of protein degradation kinetics.

# **D: Leadership and Research environment** 

My leadership experience began in 2003 when I moved to the University of York to found BioArCh, an interdisciplinary science centre based in a humanities department. I based my leadership model on the best that I experienced as a postdoctoral student (notably Prof. Steve Larter, FRS, and Prof. Peter Westbroek). I champion a team-focused, bottom-up approach to fostering scientific excellence. I think the model works; my academic family includes 12 female and 5 male Associated Profs, and 3 full Professors (two of whom, Kirsty Penkman and Beatrice Demarchi are partners on the grant) \- the third is the new director of BioArCh. BioArCh's success can be evidenced by the rising research ranking of the host Department from 23rd (2001, REF) to 4th (2014 RAE) \- one year producing 30% of all high-impact papers at the University. Currently, at the Globe Institute (UCPH) this vision continues in the development of the School of Archaeology.

The best research environments are fun, stimulating, supportive, and open. They stretch researchers to think over the horizon and support them if they stretch too far and fail. They are well-resourced but frugal (BioArCh was set up with £70k and many trips to skips and donations of furniture), open (extending to OpenSource operating systems and self-built sustainable computing), and collaborative (both internally and externally). 

As a leader, I strive to empower talented and driven researchers by removing barriers and creating opportunities. Good research leadership involves understanding and leveraging the soft power that each member of the team possesses. I use my soft power purposefully to support junior colleagues, helping them manage their soft power, and also grow their networks, lead projects, and gain proper recognition for their work, e.g. I rarely now take a senior author position on papers.

To support the next generation of research leaders, I've established @palaeome.org, a Google Workspace for Education environment that provides cloud computing and productivity tools for my students and collaborators. This platform, which I manage and fund, equips my academic family with tools for easy cooperation and overcomes the problems of researchers working between institutions. I co-founded the International Symposium for Biomolecular Archaeology, which we have transitioned into a formal society. This initiative empowers and includes a diverse new generation of scholars and breaks down divisions between major research groups.

To harvest amino acid data, Penkman\*, **PostDoc1** and I will work with Kaufmann (ASU, Arizona) and Miller (Colorado); Manica (Cambridge) will help with paleoclimate models. Long-term experimental degradation experiments will be set up at the University of York (UK; maintained and analysed by Presslee\*).

To generate the proteomes of archaeological and palaeontological fossils, Welker\*, Demarchi\*, **Technician 1, 2** and **PhD 2** will work with Sakalauskaite\* (Vilnius), Marin (Dijon), Rao\* (IVPP), and Wang (Zhejiang). **PostDoc2** (Chiang\*) will develop the *Orthrus* pipeline and will work with **PostDoc3** (w. DTU) and collaborate on software development with Dartigues (Bordeaux). 

To attract top talent we will use the UCPH palaeoproteomics summer school, the combined network of ChronoProtein researchers and collaborators, and their institutions. Using my position at Cambridge, we plan to develop a visiting PhD program and enable postdoctoral exchanges. I will develop new projects including MSCA Doctoral Training Networks in (i) Deamidation and (ii) Age At Death Estimation, each advancing the study of protein degradation in their different directions.

# **F: Research funding** 

ChronoProtein builds on novel high-risk research directions I was able to explore during my DNRF Niels Bohr Professorship, regarding the challenges of authentication, DeamiDate [(Ramsøe *et al.*, 2020\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/xgSZ), patterns of modification [(Nair *et al.*, 2023\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/cfRJ) and attempts to use MD to model hydrolysis [(Fonseca, Freeman and Collins, 2022\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/pETin). These have developed into *Orthrus* and *Vidx*. I have an ERC Proof of Concept grant with Cramer, exploring LAP-MALDI for food authentication. I have no current funding which is in any way complementary to ChronoProtein, but have applied for a smaller (dry lab) version of this with Novo Nordisk Data Science Investigator (Distinguished 2024).

Over the last 10 years, I have supervised 13 PhD students. My roles mainly involve working with them to identify what *they* need (in terms of practical, intellectual and supervision support), then giving them my time and these resources when *they* need them.

Working across two institutions, I meet each of my students every week for a minimum of 30 mins, but I am flexible to their staples of working and research. I encourage them to speak at conferences and often help introduce them to other researchers, usually via email and then by video conference. I encourage them to leave academia if I think this is appropriate but as is evident from the list above, many of them decide to stay in academia. I am lucky that so many of my former students and postdocs hold academic positions around the world linked by @palaeome.org.

# 

# **H: Other important issues**

My move to Copenhagen on a Niels Bohr Professorship represented a significant career transition that has shaped my current research focus. I have decided to stay, and now hold a dual appointment with a 50:50 split between the University of Copenhagen and the University of Cambridge. This unique position allows me to foster collaborative research across two leading institutions, bridging expertise and resources from both. I am a tax resident in Denmark, which aligns with my primary professional responsibilities and commitments, providing a stable base from which to conduct my research and engage with both academic communities effectively.

[^1]:  Geological protein decay is predictable in *closed* systems, such as proteins trapped inside biominerals, as reactants and their products cannot leak out and are therefore stable with respect to solvents and pH. Most biominerals also contain proteins (and other biomolecules) which are *open* to the burial environment and are lost as the protein decays [(Collins, 1986\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/VPHc). Closed systems are isolated by exposing powdered samples to aggressive oxidation [(Sykes, Collins and Walton, 1995\)](https://paperpile.com/c/G3vWl5/q1C3).
